ServiceNow (NOW) stock's historic sell-off looks excessive to me. The enterprise workflow software provider disappointed investors with its Q3 earnings and outlook. I understand the frustration. Yet CFO Gina Mastantuono said, "Our AI momentum continues to build," and the numbers support that view.

Subscription revenue grew 21%, while management raised its cash-flow outlook. The stock now trades at roughly 21x next year's expected earnings. That gives me a much stronger reason to look past an imperfect quarter. Thus, my NOW stock forecast is bullish.

ServiceNow's Q3 Disappointment Needs Perspective

ServiceNow's Q3 disappointment needs perspective, although the concerns are legitimate. Shares plunged following the earnings release, marking their largest one-day decline on record. Adjusted earnings per share (EPS) of $1.00 missed the $1.02 consensus. More concerning, Q4 current Remaining Performance Obligations (cRPO) growth is guided to 18.5%, against 21% constant-currency growth in Q3. That measures contracted revenue expected within 12 months, making it an important demand indicator.

Investors want proof that artificial intelligence (AI) spending will produce enough new business to sustain historical growth. A slower forward indicator makes that harder to take on faith.

Still, the latest numbers hardly suggest a broken growth engine. Subscription revenue reached $3.99 billion, up 21%. Total revenue rose 20.5% to $4.11 billion. cRPO was $13.65 billion, while total remaining obligations grew 22% to $29.7 billion.

Management raised its full-year subscription outlook and lifted its adjusted free-cash-flow margin target to 36%. Expectations were high enough that these improvements failed to satisfy investors.

Meanwhile, large customers also kept spending big. ServiceNow signed 19 transactions exceeding $5 million in net-new annual contract value (ACV), up over 135%. Customers contributing more than $5 million of ACV increased 23% to 680. I believe those commitments are a big deal.

A company losing relevance should struggle to convince major enterprises to deepen their relationships. ServiceNow is still doing that, even as investors question its future.

title: Salesforce Spent $32 Billion on Buybacks in 5 Years. Somehow, Its Share Count Still Rose
detail:
Salesforce Spent $32 Billion on Buybacks in 5 Years. Somehow, Its Share Count Still Rose
Roxanna Maglangit
Mon, November 16, 2026 at 9:35 AM CST 5 min read
CRM
Trade CRM on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Salesforce Spent $32 Billion on Buybacks in 5 Years. Somehow, Its Share Count Still Rose ©Bianca Constantinescu's Images from Canva
Key Takeaways

Salesforce spent about $32 billion on buybacks in the five fiscal years to January 2026, yet its diluted share count rose from 930 million to 956 million.

Most of that money offset stock pay and the shares Salesforce issued to buy Slack, so shareholders' slice of the company didn't grow.

In fiscal 2026, dividends and buybacks used all of Salesforce's $14.4 billion of free cash flow before the Informatica deal, and debt made up the difference.

The share count is now falling fast, but the cut is paid for with debt, so the next test is whether Salesforce can pay that debt down while stock pay keeps running.

Salesforce (CRM:NYSE) spent about $32 billion buying back its own stock in the five fiscal years to January 2026. It ended that stretch with more shares than it started with: 956 million diluted shares in fiscal 2026, against 930 million in fiscal 2021.

One investor laid this out in a post this week on the r/ValueInvesting subreddit. The post compares Salesforce with Adobe, which the poster says spent a similar $35.7 billion on buybacks and ended up with 12.1% fewer shares. Salesforce's own share counts back up the poster's numbers. And the post comes just as Salesforce is borrowing to keep its buybacks and deals going.

Stock pay and Slack ate most of it

Salesforce kept issuing new shares while it bought old ones back. Over the five years, the poster counts $15.5 billion of stock pay and $11.1 billion of stock issued to buy Slack in 2021. That's $26.6 billion of new stock in all. It's more than the $25.4 billion Salesforce spent on buybacks after subtracting the cash it took in from employee stock plans.

Diluted shares peaked at 997 million in fiscal 2023, the first full year with Slack's shares in the count. Buybacks have brought the count back down only partway since:

Salesforce (CRM): diluted shares outstanding, millions of shares, fiscal 2022-2026 (years to January) (TIKR)
The buyback is part of the pay bill

The buybacks weren't wasted. Stock pay is a real cost, and without the buybacks Salesforce's shareholders would own a smaller slice of the company today. The poster asked the thread a fair question: does a buyback that only offsets dilution count as money returned to shareholders, or as a pay cost? I'd call it a pay cost. Stock pay came to $3.5 billion in fiscal 2026, about a quarter of Salesforce's $14.4 billion of free cash flow, and it isn't taken out of that figure.
